title: When Seeking Feedback, Distinguish Between Coaching and Judging
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that the best learners distinguish between two fundamentally different kinds of feedback — coaching and judging — and actively seek the former while managing the latter. Coaching feedback is forward-looking and actionable: it identifies specific behaviors to change and provides a path to improvement. Judging feedback is retrospective and evaluative: it renders a verdict on past performance without providing a way forward. The article shows how the best learners frame their feedback requests in ways that invite coaching rather than judgment, and how this reframing changes both the quality of feedback received and the learner's relationship to the feedback process. The piece concludes that learning velocity — not raw talent — separates the fastest-improving performers, and learning velocity is a function of how intelligently one hunts for and processes developmental feedback.
points: The best learners don't wait for feedback — they hunt it down early, before results are in and while there is still time to make adjustments.
Coaching feedback is forward-looking and actionable; judging feedback is retrospective and evaluative — they serve entirely different functions in the development process.
Asking 'What's one thing I could do differently?' invites coaching; asking 'What did you think of that?' invites judgment — the framing determines what you receive.
The best learners quietly transform every feedback encounter into an opportunity for improvement rather than a moment of being evaluated and measured.
Learning velocity — not raw talent — separates the fastest-improving performers, and learning velocity is a function of how intelligently one seeks and processes feedback.
quotes: They ask questions that invite coaching, such as “What’s one thing I could do differently?” They avoid questions that invite judgments, such as “What did you think of that?” In doing so, they quietly transform the feedback they receive into an opportunity for improvement rather than a chance to be measured.

The other team member asks for specific coaching and receives a set of levers to pull: “Cut the third slide,” “slow down when presenting the data,” “rehearse for the toughest Q&A question.” This presenter walks away with a plan of action and a greater appetite for feedback next time.
But of the many practices great learners use when seeking feedback, perhaps the most important is the distinction they draw between coaching and judging.
The same piece of criticism, framed as coaching instead of judgment, becomes a source of change rather than a reason to react.
And they boil things down to one targeted change they can make instead of getting overwhelmed by a comprehensive critique.
They ask for criticism from people with differing perspectives rather than settling for the opinion closest at hand.
They tune in to what repeats, seeking patterns in feedback rather than focusing on one-off commentary.
